extracted.intended_audience: novelists and advanced students of fiction (writers studying point-of-view and method)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to render a character's inner life dramatically on the page — when to use epistolary forms or interior-point-of-view methods, how to let a mind 'act' rather than be reported, and how to choose/shape method to suit a novel's subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/diary method as showing a mind in action
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a story out of a series of letters, or a running diary written from day to day — is engaged in the attempt to show a mind in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: gives immediacy — the reader meets the character 'afresh' each day, hears the cry 'wrung from her at the moment,' and shares suspense about the next moment. It places the character's emotion and comportment under strain at the foreground. Anti-patterns/limits: on a large scale the method becomes impracticable; it forces artifices to sustain verisimilitude (e.g. keeping friends always at a distance or resorting to nested reports), which can be desperate and costly (examples: Clarissa, Grandison). Use when the subject is essentially the character's contemporaneous emotion and conduct; avoid when the logistics of correspondence would cripple the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatizing consciousness by rendering the surface movement of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist uses the look and behaviour of thought as the vehicle by which the story is rendered — the impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of telling what happened in the mind, represent the 'immediate flaw or ripple of the moment' and a series of such images so the reader sees the thought's enactment. Treat the mind's fleeting images as dramatic action: the spectator judges by appearances. This allows interior events to be dramatized without authorial exposition into 'hidden depths.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose character-point-of-view when the subject is internal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the change in a subject (e.g. Strether's change of purpose) is due to shifts in a particular character's vision, the story 'must obviously be told from [that character's] point of view' because only his consciousness can supply the necessary gradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the central event lies solely within a character's mind, render the scene through that character's senses and impressions; nothing external will give the full meaning. The author should confine the narrative to the limits of that vision so the reader shares the precise experience that effects the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the limits of the chosen point-of-view but allow subtle shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a book is seen from one man's point of view throughout, there may be 'an insidious shifting of it, so artfully contrived that the reader may arrive at the end without suspecting the trick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep primary vision with the selected character (so that scenes and descriptions are his impressions), but the author can subtly manipulate presentation so the reader sometimes attains a vantage slightly superior to the character's. Do this carefully: preserve the method's rule that everything shown is as the character sees it, while arranging moments (dialogue, framed scenes) where the character's consciousness is temporarily 'out of sight' and appears objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective exposition; favor staged, moment-by-moment revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: To announce a character's inward change with a tabulation of reasons (historic, retrospective) is undramatic; instead, 'bring his mind into view at the different moments, one after another,' and multiply these glimpses until the silent change is apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sequences of dramatic glimpses to summaries or after-the-fact accounts. This preserves suspense and allows the reader to 'have seen' the change rather than be told it. Retrospective narration risks turning demonstration into mere statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes and dialogue to supply necessary background instead of lump narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene can 'take the place of that "harking back to make up" ... which is apt to appear as a lump of narrative shortly after the opening of a story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange early scenes (e.g. conversations) that put the reader in possession of past facts through enacted speech and behaviour, rather than through expository summary. This preserves dramatic immediacy and avoids breaking the method's illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial restraint / vanish as narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should 'vanish and leave his people to act the story' — accept nothing on authority but cause the impression to be made by the characters' behaviour and thought-surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the author 'knows all there is to know' about the character, refrain from interposing that knowledge. If the author begins to expound inner substance, the reader will assume total disclosure and suspense will be lost. The narrator's part should be discreet, like a playwright arranging a scene, not an omniscient lecturer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold full interior knowledge to preserve dramatic suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator (or autobiographical narrator) is admitted into the mind 'at all he must do so without reserve' and hence would 'betray the secret that we ought to be guessing at for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow a narrator who, by position, would be expected to give full disclosure to begin revealing inner substance piecemeal; either fully disclose (which kills suspense) or continue to dramatize surface impressions. Use dramatization to play the story out 'by due degrees' to keep deliberation, refrainment and suspension intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply dramatic principles to description — make a drama of the picture
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic rule is applied more fundamentally; it animates the actual elements of the picture, the description, and makes a drama of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject matter is undramatic in literal action, use dramatizing devices to animate description itself — treat descriptive passages as enactments, not mere background. But do not fake drama by inserting trivial or unnecessary dialogue; that cheapens characters and reduces impact when real drama is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pepper the surface with irrelevant animated dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not managed by peppering the surface with animated dialogue, by making the characters break into talk when they really have nothing to contribute to the subject; the end of this is only to cheapen and discredit their talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use spoken exchange when it genuinely furthers the subject's dramatic effect. Superfluous talk weakens later moments when real speech is required and undermines the method's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method choice should serve the subject's highest relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the novelist's ingenuity is always the same; it is to give to his subject the highest relief by which it is capable of profiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and combine methods (epistolary, interior dramatization, scenic dialogue) with the aim of maximizing the subject's expressive potential. Be aware of the newly available resources (e.g. dramatized consciousness) and consider inventive mixtures, but measure choices against their effect on the subject rather than novelty alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of verisimilitude costs when adopting constrained methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Richardson 'pays with the desperate shifts to which he is driven in order to maintain any kind of verisimilitude' when he confines action to letters and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a method imposes constraints (letters, diaries, single consciousness), examine the plausible logistics: keeping other characters at a distance, nested reports, or strained explanations may be necessary to sustain the form but can erode credibility. Weigh these costs against the method's dramatic advantages.
